itinerary.cal: Requires a car or bike shuttle between the Lena Lake and Putvin trailheads (~4 mi apart on Hamma Hamma River Road); best done July-September once the high traverse and gullies are mostly clear of snow.

Off-trail, exposed, and long — this is the crux day.

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 3-day, ~16-mile alpine traverse with two backcountry camps (Upper Lena Lake, then Lake of the Angels) and roughly 8,400-9,000 ft of cumulative gain; very strong parties instead push the whole loop car-to-car in a single ~14-16 hour day.

before.overview: A long, mostly off-trail traverse linking Upper Lena Lake to Mount Stone via St. Peter's Gate, connecting several alpine lakes and basins in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness before finishing on Stone's west ridge. It is a full, demanding day out rather than a technical climb — mostly maintained trail and way-trail, with legitimate scrambling on loose glacial material near the high point.
hazards: Extensive off-trail/way-trail route-finding over multiple ridges
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate
A very long day (up to 16 miles, ~9,000 ft gain) with limited bail options partway through
Fog/whiteout navigation risk on Mount Stone's upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route in fog and ended up in unplanned, harder terrain.
Exposed headwall section(s) with several-hundred-foot drop-offs near the Lena Lake/Lake of the Angels basin transition; some parties use a fixed handline or tree roots.
Unbridged stream crossings requiring down-climbing to the streambed and back up on the way-trail sections.
before.approach: Start at the Lena Lake Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~600-750 ft). Follow the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail (#810) about 3 miles through second-growth and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft), a popular backpacking destination with reliable camping and water. Beyond Lena Lake the trail narrows to a steep, primitive tread that climbs the West Fork Lena Creek drainage; continue roughly 3.5 more miles and about 2,200 additional feet to Upper Lena Lake (~4,000 ft total gain, ~6.5 mi from the trailhead), the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp before the traverse goes cross-country. From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head southwest/west: pick up the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and huckleberry-heather slopes past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass (~5,200 ft), descend slightly to Upper Scout Lake, contour high around it into Scout Basin, and climb to Ullin's Pass (~5,000 ft) overlooking the tarns known as "Ullin's Bathtubs." From Ullin's Pass, a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp that angles across a steep hillside below Mt. Stone and ends at a loose, grungy moraine; the final approach to St. Peter's Gate (~5,950 ft, the traverse's high point) is exposed dirt-and-mud slopes with real route-finding demands, about 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake. This entire off-trail section crosses loose moraine and talus, can hold snow patches well into summer (many parties carry an ice axe), and has no dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the small tarns near Ullin's Pass; fog is common and has caused parties to lose the route. From St. Peter's Gate, most parties cache overnight packs and descend about 300 ft to the base of a basalt cliff, then follow a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mt. Stone's south face into a rock bowl below the summit block, joining the standard west-ridge route for a final ~100 ft of Class 2-3 scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the true (south) summit.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake, Upper Lena Lake and the way-trails to St. Peter's Gate
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at about 750 ft, the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail #810 runs about 3 miles through second- and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Beyond the lake the trail narrows to steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage, roughly 3.5 more miles and 2,200 ft to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft — 6.5 miles and about 4,000 ft from the road, the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp.

From Upper Lena Lake the traverse goes cross-country: the Scout Lake way-trail west across meadows and huckleberry-heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake, contour high round it into Scout Basin, then up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft overlooking Ullin's Bathtubs. From Ullin's Pass a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp angling across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending at a loose grungy moraine, then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft — roughly 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake.

No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Scout Pass and Ullin's Pass are largely clear; many parties still carry an axe

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE SUMMIT CLIMB IS 300 FT BELOW ST. PETER'S GATE, AND THE FIRST MOVE IS DOWNHILL — WHICH IS THE WHOLE TEST. Reach the Gate (the traverse's high point at about 5,950 ft, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge). Cache your overnight packs there. Then DESCEND ABOUT 300 FT to the BASE OF A BASALT CLIFF. The climber's path up the south-face gully starts at the foot of that cliff. A route that goes up from the Gate is not this one.

That is a good fog test precisely because it is counter-intuitive: standing in a notch with the summit above you, the instruction is to lose height first and pick the line up from underneath the cliff band.

SECOND TEST, in the gully: it is a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mount Stone's SOUTH face, and it leads into a ROCK BOWL below the summit block. The bowl is the confirmation — an enclosed basin of rock, not a ridge and not open slope. From it the line joins the standard west-ridge route for a final 100 ft or so of Class 2-3 scrambling on SOLID PILLOW BASALT to the true south summit. That last detail is worth trusting: the rock at the top of this peak is noticeably better than anything below it, so if the last hundred feet is still rubble you have not reached the summit ridge.

WHAT GOES WRONG HERE, AND IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL: fog is common on Mount Stone's upper mountain and multiple parties have lost the route and ended up in unplanned harder terrain, and in cloud the true south summit is confused with the Middle and North summits. Count your summits and do not accept the first one.

EXIT NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE PLAN, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the standard finish continues southwest half a mile to the Lake of the Angels basin and out the Putvin Trail — a DIFFERENT trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake. Arrange a shuttle or stash a bike before you start.

itinerary.cal: Overnight camping at Lake of the Angels is inside Olympic National Park (a wilderness permit is required), but it's a heavily used, fragile alpine basin — camp on durable/established sites only.

before.approach: From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~1,600 ft), the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail (no official number) that climbs steeply and directly from the start — expect root-staircase steps and a boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. About halfway up, the trail meets a rock headwall that requires hand-over-hand climbing; a large tree root serves as the key handhold, and on at least one especially steep pitch a fixed handline rope has historically been in place to assist. Above the headwall the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet before reaching Lake of the Angels (~4,850 ft) in a dramatic cirque below Mt. Stone's south face and the St. Peter's Gate notch — about 3 miles and roughly 3,000 ft of gain from the road. There is little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake, and expect the trail to be slick when wet and to hold snow on shaded steps into early summer. From the lake, contour/climb toward St. Peter's Gate; just before the gate, turn sharply left (south) and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in Mt. Stone's west ridge. Turn right at the notch and climb directly toward it, arriving at a first sub-summit rock; climb a short, low-Class-3 chimney to its top, cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove in the rock on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the summit. The route is Class 3 throughout (rated Grade I in the Olympic Mountains climbing guide); from Lake of the Angels camp, figure roughly 2.5 hours up to the summit.

waypoints.directions: Park at the unmarked pullout on Hamma Hamma River Road (Forest Service Road 25), about 1,600 feet, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake trailhead. A slide near road mile 10.5 has at times closed the last 1.2 miles of the road; check current Forest Service status, since a closure would add a road walk to reach the pullout. The Putvin Trail itself is an unmaintained, primitive user path with no official number, and it starts climbing steeply right from the road.

before.approach: Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813, ~1,565 ft) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25) — note that in recent years a slide/washout near mile 10.5 has at times blocked the final ~1.2 miles of road, forcing an extra road-walk to the actual trailhead, so check current Forest Service status before you go. From the trailhead the Putvin Trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek for a few hundred feet, then launches into a long, unrelenting climbing traverse to the west — this trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles and does not ease up. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an old logging road (the tread is easy to lose here; look for the trail continuation slightly downhill) and enters the Skokomish Wilderness/Olympic National Park boundary. Around 4,200 ft there is a short but notable headwall/rock step with an old hand-line (or a large exposed tree root used as a handhold) to surmount slick rock — the crux of the trail itself and a common turnaround point for unprepared hikers, especially wet. The maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles (~4,500 ft, sometimes called Frog/Fawn Pond), where a rougher way-trail continues up steep, rocky terrain to Lake of the Angels (~4,900 ft), reached around 4 miles in. Snow typically lingers on the north-facing basin above Lake of the Angels well into summer (consolidated snow reported from ~4,500 ft on), so an ice axe (and sometimes microspikes/crampons) is worth carrying into early-mid summer. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail and goes cross-country: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet of rocky, brushy ground, then traverses up beneath St. Peter's Gate (the pass southeast of the summit) and back west to a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge; from the notch, class 3 scrambling leads a couple of hundred feet to a shallow hanging basin, then continue through talus/boulder terrain toward the summit block. Total one-way distance is about 4.8 miles with roughly 5,053 ft of gain to the 6,618 ft high point. Hazards: reliable water is available along Boulder Creek and at Lake of the Angels but is scarce above the lake; the gully/rib terrain above the lake is loose and route-finding is nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow; the lower trail's root/rock headwall is genuinely exposed when wet.
